editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

div0.head: Interview with Edgar Grabhorn on October 9, 2000

div1.p: The following oral history testimony is the result of an audiotaped interview with Edgar Grabhorn, conducted by Wynn Wilbur on October 9, 2000, on behalf of the Veterans' Oral History Project. The interview took place in Concord (Mass?) and is part of the Library of Congress collection of oral testimonies.
The Interview was transcribed and processed by Victoria L. Pittman, RPR.

The reader should bear in mind that she or he is reading a verbatim transcript of spoken, rather than written prose. Insofar as possible, this transcript tries to represent the spoken word. Thus, it should be read as a personal memoir and not as either a researched monograph or edited account.

To the extent possible, the spelling of place names, foreign words and personal names have been verified, either by reference resources or directly by the interviewee. Some uncertainties will inevitably remain regarding some words and their spellings. In these scenarios, a (ph) follows a word or name that is spelled phonetically.
div1.div2:
Wynn Wilbur
This is an interview with Edgar Grabhorn who was in the Air Force during World War II, Korea, and the Vietnam conflict. The interview is being held for the Concord Historical Commission's Oral History Project on October 9, 2000, at the home of Wynn Wilbur, who is the interviewer. Wynn Wilbur
Mr. Grabhorn is presently 70- Edgar Grabhorn
-6. Wynn Wilbur
-6 years old. So, Ed, tell us how you happened to get into the service back in World War II years. Edgar Grabhorn
I was in high school in 1941, just graduating as a senior, and the War started. I was still too -- I was 17, still too young to get into the service, so I went off to Purdue -- that was my original plan, anyway, was to get an engineering degree at Purdue. In fact, get a mechanical engineering degree and go design automobiles in Detroit. In the course of my enrollment at Purdue, I saw that I could become an Aviation Cadet after I was 18 and go off to fly if I was called. So I did. I joined the Aviation Cadets in the fall of 1942. And -- thinking the war would be over before I would ever get called to active duty. But shortly -- in the spring, I did get called to active duty and went off to learn to fly airplanes. So that's how I got into the service. I didn't intend to be a career person in the military, but as you'll hear later on, things conspired to keep me in and so I did. Wynn Wilbur
When did you -- when did you go overseas? How long were you in training and then what happened? Edgar Grabhorn
I got my wings in 1943, late in 1943, and was commissioned as Second Lieutenant and a navigator and received orders to go off to a bomb group, to join a crew and commence training for ultimate combat -- combat duty. I went home for a brief vacation, a week or so, and then joined a group in Alamogordo, New Mexico, a four-engine bomb group. Became the missing member of the -- of the crew. They had all the other crew members in place, gunners and engineers and pilots and bombardier, and just needed a navigator. And so I filled that role. We left Alamogordo in March, heading overseas. It was wintertime still in the North Atlantic, so our bomb group was routed down through South America, Africa, and then up to England. So it was a long and very educational tour for a farm boy from Indiana. We went to Puerto Rico, we went to Trinidad, and down along the northern coast of Brazil. Got to Natal, waited a couple days for winds to be favorable and then flew across to Dakar in Africa, Senegal. Then from there up, like the French Foreign Legion, up across the desert. In fact, past Tindu, where they filmed some of the old Foreign Legion films, and then to Marrakesh. Marrakesh, again, we waited for the weather a little bit and then flew out over Casablanca, north along Portugal, and finally reached England. All that took a couple weeks. We got to the west coast of England, I navigated all the way from Africa. And I was term dead tired, and so were the rest of the crew members, and we were met and said that we were going to fly -- get back into our airplane and fly cross England to our air base. We practically revolted. But they said, Well, nothing to it, you just follow me and when we wiggle our wings, it will be time for you to go down to your base.
(Laughter) Edgar Grabhorn
(Laughter) We went into -- we followed along. I had -- I had a map, and so I followed them along. I thought, Well, at least I'll keep track of airfields. Wynn Wilbur
This is a really dumb question, but did they have radar then? Edgar Grabhorn
No, no radar. Wynn Wilbur
So you really were telling them where to go. Edgar Grabhorn
Right. Yeah. Oh, yeah. You had to look out. If you couldn't see something, you did it by what's called dead reckoning. In any case, we got over our airfield, he wiggled his wings and we went in and landed. And sure enough, there was the rest of our bomb group. Did a couple more weeks of training. We began flying combat missions, and... Wynn Wilbur
This is the spring of '44? Edgar Grabhorn
Uh-huh. Wynn Wilbur
So you were flying into Germany. Edgar Grabhorn
Yeah. Our mission -- Wynn Wilbur
_____________ (undecipherable). Edgar Grabhorn
Our missions were -- well, combat started immediately because France was still occupied by the Germans, and so was Holland and Belgium. So we -- we had targets all over. we had targets in France, we had targets in Belgium, railway yards and things like that. And then, of course, targets all over Germany. I flew until my -- on my 11th mission, we were bombing an oil refinery, we did bomb an oil refinery northeast of Berlin, and because it was so deep into Germany, our fighter escort couldn't stay with us, they didn't have enough fuel. And the Germans loved that, because their fighters came up and... Wynn Wilbur
Uh-huh. Edgar Grabhorn
-- and beat us up. And so I was shot down by a German fighter, or our crew was shot down. And I was in various prisons and hospitals and that sort of thing until Patton came into Germany in 1945. I was liberated in April 1945 from what became East Germany and taken out on a stretcher to Frankfurt, and put into a smaller airplane and flown to Paris, where they put me in a hospital. And I was -- I was there for, for a month sort of regaining my health. And then moved to a British hospital in Salisbury, England. And I was there almost another month. And then put on a British hospital ship in July and brought back to the States. Wynn Wilbur
July of '45? Edgar Grabhorn
July 1945. Wynn Wilbur
And am I correct in thinking that when you were shot down, your leg was very badly broken, shattered and -- Edgar Grabhorn
I -- Wynn Wilbur
-- there was a German surgeon who -- who decided not to amputate? Edgar Grabhorn
Yeah. I -- I, my leg -- I was shot up while still in the airplane. Among the other things the fighters did, they pretty well riddled our airplane. Wynn Wilbur
Oh, how horrible. Edgar Grabhorn
And actually, my leg collapsed under me. I was laying on the floor in the font part of the airplane where the navigator's stationed, and -- thinking that I was really trapped. And the rest of the crew was sort of collecting around the flight deck. And the next thing I know, I'm out in the air. The airplane had been apparently exploded. Wynn Wilbur
Oh. Edgar Grabhorn
Because all I could see of the airplane was from one engine out toward the one wing tip, sort of whirling around going down to the water. This was over the Baltic Sea. And there were three other parachutes that were out in the air besides my own. Yes, my leg was shot up. After I got fished out of the water by a German freighter the next day and taken to East Prussia, put in a naval hospital where the doctor there said that he'd amputate my leg when he had time, but he was still busy with Germans. And the next day, without doing anything, changing dressings that I'd put on or anything else, they put me in a vehicle and took me across the country to a German Luftwaffe hospital. Wynn Wilbur
Oh. Edgar Grabhorn
Apparently they decided that I wasn't in the jurisdiction of the Navy, that I should be under the Air Force. And they took put me into that hospital, and there I met a really wonderful doctor who looked at my leg and he said, "I should amputate, but I'll try to save your leg. If I'm unsuccessful, it'll be cut off much higher than it would be right now." And he wanted to know what I felt about that. And I said "I'd appreciate having my leg." And he did. He did a wonderful job. It was a long _____. Wynn Wilbur
Well, considering that you are in the process of hiking across all of Massachusetts, I'm sure you're very glad to have your leg. Edgar Grabhorn
Oh, very much. And although it took a long time, I was in the hospitals and prison camps, and then back in the States in other military hospitals until early 1947 I was finally released back onto active duty. Wynn Wilbur
_______. Edgar Grabhorn
Yeah. I developed a bone infection when I was in prison, and that took a long time to sanitize and clear up, including bone grafts and skin grafts and that kind of thing. But in any case, I went back on flying duty in 1947. Wynn Wilbur
Did at -- some point after the War, you went back and met that surgeon again, didn't you? Edgar Grabhorn
I did. Much later in my career, in 1950, I was flying in and out of Germany quite frequently from Westover, actually, over in western Massachusetts. And I had an address -- he had corresponded with my mother. I had given him my home address, and he'd corresponded. She'd sent him food packages and clothing and all sorts of other stuff. And I had that address, and so I searched him out and found him to be a successful surgeon in a small hospital near Cologne. And naturally, we had many fine reminiscences, talking about what had happened -- Wynn Wilbur
Checking your leg. Edgar Grabhorn
-- what had happened to each of us in the meanwhile. But, yeah, it's sure good to have a leg. Wynn Wilbur
So in 1947 when you went back into active duty, were you flying again? There was no war at that point. Edgar Grabhorn
Not immediately. To explain why I was still in the military in 1947, I wanted to get out of the military in the worst way, like all civilian military people, but I couldn't because my leg was wounded, and there I was. And by 1947, I had gone back to Purdue and found that where our freshman class was a thousand and had been the largest class Purdue had ever had, the campus had 10,000 students on it. It was a vast school compared to what it was when I was there, and I -- wasn't all that attractive to me to go back to school. Wynn Wilbur
Wow. Edgar Grabhorn
And I liked to fly. Turned out I really enjoyed flying. So I decided, Well, you know, this is not a bad life. I'll just try it for a little while longer. And that's why I stayed in. Wynn Wilbur
You stayed in eventually until 1970-something. Edgar Grabhorn
'69. End of 1969. I -- I was still not really decided about my career, but my next assignment after 1947 was to Hawaii. I had a wonderful three years in Hawaii. Met my present wife, who was a -- an Army officer's daughter. And had some wonderful flying. We -- we laughingly called our group the Fungus Airlines. We flew to every island in the Pacific, which was very entertaining and interesting places you will -- you'll never go, probably -- Christmas Island and Palmyra Island and things like that -- but it was a -- it was a great experience. Wynn Wilbur
Why were you flying to these places? Edgar Grabhorn
Supplies had to be delivered, and sometimes for emergency situations, where people had to be air evac'd out from those places and so we'd go do that. Wynn Wilbur
Did the United States keep occupying little units on all these places after the War? Edgar Grabhorn
They did. Sometimes they were stations for radio aids to navigation where there would be just a transmitting station there, but had to be maintained and people kept it up and people were there on these rocks. Eniwetok as you know, became a big test site for atomic weapons. Kwajalein, Guam, we went down to the Fijis and Samoa on our way to turn around in Australia. And it's a vast ocean. And, and the navigator has a very important job, which was also interesting. Wynn Wilbur
But by then, you did have radar, didn't you? Edgar Grabhorn
We did have radar. It was -- it was not the greatest, but it was radar that had been developed during War II, that's right. I was in Hawaii in 1948 and offered a regular commission in the Air Force, and that's when division -- decision day really happened. I accepted it. And shortly after that, Secretary Johnson, who was Secretary of Defense at the time, had a big reduction in force. They couldn't see that there was going to be any war on the horizon, and so our -- our groups all condensed down to just a few members. Wynn Wilbur
Hmm. Edgar Grabhorn
In 1950, when the Korean War started, I was just finishing my tour in Hawaii, had my orders to come back to Westover and fly on the North Atlantic. And I was put on the -- along with three other navigators -- put on the last boat that carried people off of Hawaii. Everyone else was frozen on the island at the beginning of the Korean War. They even talked about coming out by helicopter and picking us up and taking us back. Wynn Wilbur
A long helicopter ride. Edgar Grabhorn
(Laughter) In any case, I no sooner got to Westover, assigned to transport duty flying to Europe, then we were sent Temporary Duty back to Hawaii. (Laughter) Wynn Wilbur
And then off to Korea. Were you married by then? Edgar Grabhorn
No, no. Marion and I were seriously dating. I had -- I had an airplane of my own in Northampton, and later when I came off the run from flying transports, I'd jump into my little single-engine airplane, fly down to Washington, DC, date Marion, whose father was then stationed in the Pentagon, then I'd fly back up and then go back on the run again. Wynn Wilbur
Oh. So -- Edgar Grabhorn
So I did a minimum -- we all did minimum tours in those days. We could plan -- we could plan that within 12 months of being assigned to the States, we'd be on our way back out again. And my assignment then was to Japan to fly reconnaissance for the Korean War. Wynn Wilbur
So this is now 1950? Edgar Grabhorn
1950. Wynn Wilbur
All of '50? Edgar Grabhorn
1952 I ended up in Japan and started flying in RV29s, which was -- had been a big bombing airplane in War II and was developed into a reconnaissance airplane as well as a bomber. Wynn Wilbur
Oh. Edgar Grabhorn
We flew 15-hour missions. People talk about long flights being eight hours these days, and it's laughing to think of very commonly flying for 15 hours. Wynn Wilbur
I'm sure the seats weren't as comfortable. Edgar Grabhorn
Aw. Wynn Wilbur
And you didn't get up and walk down the aisle. Edgar Grabhorn
Oh, so tedious. Yeah. Wynn Wilbur
How many -- Edgar Grabhorn
We flew in wetsuits, too. Wynn Wilbur
Oh. Edgar Grabhorn
You realize you're flying in a rubberized suit that's -- Wynn Wilbur
Oh. Edgar Grabhorn
-- cuffed around your arms and your legs, but you can only last -- you could only last 30 minutes in that water, if you went down in the Japan Sea you -- Wynn Wilbur
It was that cold? Edgar Grabhorn
It was that cold. And so we were uncomfortable, but we wore them, wetsuits, the whole time we flew. Wynn Wilbur
Geez. Edgar Grabhorn
Until we came out of _______. Wynn Wilbur
I guess. Where were you -- now, this was 1952. Edgar Grabhorn
1952. Wynn Wilbur
So you were flying the DMZ or where? Edgar Grabhorn
We had three -- three basic missions we flew. We flew down over the China Sea and then all along the Chinese coast, up and over Korea, and then back down to Japan, was one -- one mission we flew. Another one was strictly to go out to Korea and do continuing recon -- reconnaissance over Korea, North and South Korea. Generally tried to stay south of -- of the DMZ, but many cases we went over it. And then we had another one where we flew from Japan, up the Kuril Islands, which are a chain of islands that run up to Petropavlovsk in eastern Russia, then we flew up there and then turned around, flew back. The Russians were based heavily along there. In fact, very frequently had fighters jump up to come after us. And all we had to do was turn out over the Pacific and they would turn around and go back. Wynn Wilbur
Oh. Edgar Grabhorn
Because they weren't about to get very far from home. Wynn Wilbur
Did the Chinese fly and try to attack your plane? Edgar Grabhorn
Beg your pardon? Wynn Wilbur
Did the Chinese have -- Edgar Grabhorn
We shot at. Wynn Wilbur
-- fighters who tried to -- Edgar Grabhorn
We got shot at on the China Sea from boats, yeah. Wynn Wilbur
From boats? Edgar Grabhorn
From boats. Wynn Wilbur
Yeah. Edgar Grabhorn
They never hit us. Wynn Wilbur
They didn't have fighter planes, though that you -- Edgar Grabhorn
No, they didn't come out with fighters, just boats. Wynn Wilbur
Was your job as -- in recon also to be bombing convoys of things if you see them coming -- Edgar Grabhorn
No. Wynn Wilbur
-- down -- Edgar Grabhorn
We carried no weapons other than machine guns to fight off fighters. Wynn Wilbur
So, attacks. Edgar Grabhorn
Yeah. No, we didn't ever carry bombs. It was strictly reconnaissance. we had lots of reconnaissance equipment on our airplane. Wynn Wilbur
So you were photographing changes -- Edgar Grabhorn
And -- and sensing radio signals and things like that, what's called ELINT, electronic intelligence. And we had another device on our airplane that was used to collect debris from atomic explosions so that if we were flying along the Kuril Islands and the Russians had set off an A test, the debris that from that would float in the atmosphere and we would collect particles and bring them back to be analyzed. Wynn Wilbur
Collect it where? Edgar Grabhorn
In the air. In the air. Wynn Wilbur
I mean what -- you didn't put it inside the plane, you had some kind of -- Edgar Grabhorn
Well, these devices had, sort of, filters -- Wynn Wilbur
Uh-huh. Edgar Grabhorn
-- that you would stick up in the collector. And periodically you'd change them. yeah, you'd load the -- put the filters down in here. Wynn Wilbur
God. That sounds so dangerous. Edgar Grabhorn
(Laughter) Well, maybe it does now, but in those days, okay, so there's a guy back there catching bugs. (Laughter) Wynn Wilbur
Oh, dear Lord. It's a miracle you're walking around. Edgar Grabhorn
And of course, a lot of times on those missions, we were sent out when our intelligence knew the Russians had just set off an atomic -- Wynn Wilbur
I see. Edgar Grabhorn
-- test. Wynn Wilbur
So you were definitely -- that was your purpose. Edgar Grabhorn
That was what we were there for on that -- that mission, yeah. The other missions were in support -- direct support of the war. But that was a -- collecting -- well, we also collected weather data. You know, there's no -- there was no intelligence for weather in the Kuril Islands other than what we brought back. So we measured winds, we measured temperature, and all the other weather effects you can possibly measure. Wynn Wilbur
Whoo. Edgar Grabhorn
It was interesting. Wynn Wilbur
I bet. By 1952, it was -- the war was kind of a stalemate, wasn't it? Edgar Grabhorn
It was. Wynn Wilbur
There were -- Edgar Grabhorn
'52 and '53. Wynn Wilbur
-- little forays, and people would get killed -- Edgar Grabhorn
Yeah. Remember, the Marines marched right up the -- to the _______. Wynn Wilbur
Yeah. _______. Edgar Grabhorn
And then the Chinese got involved and -- and got driven back, but it was in that time. And -- Wynn Wilbur
That was -- that was the winter of '51, wasn't it? Edgar Grabhorn
'51. Wynn Wilbur
Yeah. Edgar Grabhorn
And then they sat up there in the winter and -- Wynn Wilbur
Along the 38? Edgar Grabhorn
You know, the negotiations got started. And, let's see when did MacArthur make his Inchon landing? Wynn Wilbur
That was early on. That was before y'all -- Edgar Grabhorn
Yeah. Yeah. We were flying -- I was flying -- Wynn Wilbur
Back and forth there? Edgar Grabhorn
Temporary Duty then, yeah. Wynn Wilbur
Were you there in 1950 as well as in '52? Edgar Grabhorn
1950, '51, '52 -- Wynn Wilbur
All those years. Edgar Grabhorn
I was flying Temporary Duty. Wynn Wilbur
What does that mean? Edgar Grabhorn
Well, my permanent station was Westover, but they -- they took -- Wynn Wilbur
You just happened to be in Japan. Edgar Grabhorn
They took a whole bunch of us in airplanes -- airplanes and all, and moved us out to Hawaii because there weren't many around, you know, there really weren't -- we didn't have many transports. And we would pick up a load of Marines with their packs and everything, 75 of them, and take them into Pusan. Wynn Wilbur
I see. Edgar Grabhorn
And then we'd bring them out on stretchers, the ones that were wounded. They just -- we'd just convert the inside of our airplane to be stretcher -- Wynn Wilbur
Right. Edgar Grabhorn
Stretcher bearing. Bring them back either to Hawaii or sometimes clear back to the west coast. Wynn Wilbur
Did you also help in the landing at Inchon, or was that all -- Edgar Grabhorn
No. Wynn Wilbur
-- by sea? Edgar Grabhorn
No, no. Wynn Wilbur
That was all water? Edgar Grabhorn
Yeah, that was not us. The flying duty really was for the most part carrying troops and supplies, some. Wynn Wilbur
So then when that were was -- Edgar Grabhorn
So, I finally convinced my commander that, "You got to let me go back to the States and get married". Wynn Wilbur
Uh-huh. Edgar Grabhorn
I went back on Temporary Duty -- now that you know what that is -- told Marion I was coming, and she arranged that we would be married at -- her father's station then was Fort Bliss in El Paso. Wynn Wilbur
Uh-huh. Edgar Grabhorn
And we were married in the base chapel in 1953 on an engine change. Wynn Wilbur
(Laughter) Edgar Grabhorn
I had brought an airplane back that needed to have an engine changed, and they changed it at -- in Oklahoma, and so that gave me time, while they changed that, tested it out, flight tested, and -- Wynn Wilbur
Did that give you a week or 12 hours? Edgar Grabhorn
More -- more than a week. We went down to Acapulco, had a nice honeymoon, and went up to San Francisco, where I met my crew again. And I thought it was going to be simple, that Marion would just -- to put on a troop transport or a military vehicle of some kind, maybe fly, and join me in -- in Japan. Turns out the rules weren't that straightforward, that -- it said, I found out later, that it was your responsibility to deliver your new wife to your duty station. From there on, they would ship her with you. Wynn Wilbur
And that was Westover. Edgar Grabhorn
No, my duty station then was Japan. Wynn Wilbur
Oh, I see. Edgar Grabhorn
I'm now permanently in Japan until next set of orders. Wynn Wilbur
So that was your nickel. Edgar Grabhorn
So I -- I bought her a Pan Am ticket, and -- took her 24 hours of flying to get from San Francisco to Japan -- and she joined me. So we were there until 1955, and in '55, we both flew back together to my -- back to my next duty station, which was down in Mississippi. Wynn Wilbur
And one of your children was born there. Edgar Grabhorn
No, she was 7 months pregnant when we left Japan with our first child, with Cliff. So Cliff was born in Mississippi. Wynn Wilbur
Mississippi? Edgar Grabhorn
Our next one was born in Massachusetts. Our next one was born in Mississippi. And our next one back in Massachusetts. (Laughter). Wynn Wilbur
Back and forth. Edgar Grabhorn
Well, in between, I did duty in Europe and I -- our electronics training center was at Keesler Air Force Base in Biloxi, Mississippi. So being in electronics, which I took up shortly after War II, I was regularly trained or advanced in training at Biloxi. So then the Korean War ended. I came home shortly after the Korean War -- after the truce was signed. And in fact, the truce with Japan was finally signed in -- in '53, I think it was, while I was there. We were Army of Occupation, originally, while I was there, and then the truce signed, we became a slightly different, hard-to-tell-the-difference troop, status. Wynn Wilbur
What was it like living in Japan during those years, eight or ten years, after the war? Edgar Grabhorn
Good point. Because I was a -- newly married in 1953, the Air Force did not provide base quarters for us, either. Wynn Wilbur
Oh. Edgar Grabhorn
So I had a Japanese contractor build me a Japanese-style house out in the rice paddies, and Marion and I -- Wynn Wilbur
With sliding doors? Edgar Grabhorn
Yeah, with sliding doors. Wynn Wilbur
Oh, that's wonderful. Edgar Grabhorn
And tatami on the floor and the whole works. And we lived a year out in the rice paddies before base housing finally came to our lowly status.
Wynn Wilbur
How romantic, though. Edgar Grabhorn
(Laughter). Well, the thing is, Japan was still very feudal in those days. If you went out in the countryside, which we did a lot of, we -- we did a lot of skiing up in the northern part of Japan, we did a lot of touring around, because we had no children, we had that freedom, and you didn't go very far from Tokyo, and you were out into a feudal time. You saw no people in western dress. They were all wearing their traditional clothing, and they were all simple people, farming and... Wynn Wilbur
Could you speak any Japanese? Edgar Grabhorn
I did. I took two college semesters of Japanese while I was there in Japan at Yokota. And I learned to write, because I liked the calligraphy, being interested in art. Wynn Wilbur
Yeah. Edgar Grabhorn
And I learned, well, 500 congis, very -- very fluently, which is the equivalent of about the third grade in school. (Laughter). Wynn Wilbur
But you could cover your basic, where is the chicken or could you tell me -- Edgar Grabhorn
Exactly. Well, I could carry on conversation without any trouble at all, yeah, yeah. I -- I would occasionally misuse the words. I wanted to buy -- Wynn Wilbur
There are tenses, are there, present and past? Isn't -- Edgar Grabhorn
It's -- there is. And it's a very -- it's a very rigorous language. You can tell -- the subject is set aside by a special sound, the direct object is set aside by a special sound, the verb is always at the end. They have a special sound for question mark, so there's no doubt at all when someone asks you a question. Ee carda deska (ph), for example, ends in "ka," ka is the sound of the question mark. So I would ask you "How are you?" and you know that because the ka sound. If you were making an exclamation, you would end the sentence with "ga," which, again, says -- Wynn Wilbur
Great. Edgar Grabhorn
-- I just went, "exclamation mark." But it's a lot of fun, it's a very -- it's a simple language in that it is 50 sounds, no unusual sounds at all. Very phonetic and easy. Wynn Wilbur
Does it have the four tones that Chinese has? Edgar Grabhorn
No. No. No tonal change at all. In fact, Japanese, if you listen to them, there's pretty much of a monotone, occasional inflection, but not much. But that -- that was a very fascinating thing. And by this time, I'm a regular officer and I'm a Captain, and things are shaping up. Shortly afterwards, returning to the States, I became a Major and moved a couple of grades to field grade, which makes a big difference. I didn't realize what a difference it would make. Wynn Wilbur
What does that mean? Edgar Grabhorn
It means that I could call the motor pool and be pretty sure I could get a staff car when I wanted one -- Wynn Wilbur
That's nice. Edgar Grabhorn
-- for example. Wynn Wilbur
Uh-huh. Edgar Grabhorn
I no longer had to pull officer of the duty [sic] kind of duty. I was freed of that. You -- well, there were a lot of -- there were many -- there were many perks of being a field grade officer. Wynn Wilbur
Uh-huh. Edgar Grabhorn
The Air Force, you were asking -- or going to ask the question, "How did it affect your life?" The Air Force did all it could to train its officers, and they sent me back to finish my college degree, which was great. Wynn Wilbur
Oh. Edgar Grabhorn
I went back got my double-A degree, got part of -- Wynn Wilbur
Was that at Purdue, or was that -- Edgar Grabhorn
No, I ended up going to Oklahoma University, and -- it was closer to where I was. So I benefited by that as well. Wynn Wilbur
______ just as many other people got through college by GI Bill. _____ staying in and _____ Edgar Grabhorn
Similar to that, and I could have done that. I could have done the GI Bill if I'd not stayed in. Wynn Wilbur
Yeah. So you had what sounds like very serene years between '53 and when they were -- Edgar Grabhorn
Yeah, except for flying, except for the combat duty, and up to '55, it was great. Then came back to Westover to be the electronics officer for a squadron in West -- at Westover. And a friend of mine and fellow officer that I had served with a couple of times called me one day from the Pentagon, where he was a personnel officer, and said, How would I like to have duty in Germany? Wynn Wilbur
Oh. Edgar Grabhorn
And he said, family accompany and so on, and I said, "Sounds great". And he said, "Okay, well, you'll -- you'll get orders pretty soon and -- and you'll go. You'll find it a -- a very different assignment. We can't talk about it, but you'll find it a very different assignment." And with that, I did get orders to a special reconnaissance group in Germany that -- headquarters, Air Force, in Wiesbaden. And this assignment, to show how different it was, I drove my station wagon with our two children and my wife to New York.
END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE; BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE. Edgar Grabhorn
'57, we moved into a state room that had been occupied by Chief Justice Earl Warren on the trip back from Europe, so you know it wasn't half bad. And we danced our way to Germany. We had a wonderful time on that trip, it was a smooth ride, and at Bremershaven (sic.), they unloaded my car and we climbed in and drove to Wiesbaden. At Wiesbaden, there were no quarters to -- for everyone in Germany, and so they had leased houses out in the community. We were assigned to one of the townhouse of the Prince of Hesse. I counted the rooms in that house one time, there are 50 rooms altogether. On the top floor was the hausmeister and his wife, next floor down was the finance minister for Wiesbaden -- or land Hesse, actually. Then Marion and I occupied what would be the piano nobile in Italy. The next floor and down on the bottom floor was a follow officer, a major and his wife, had no children. But we had a wonderful time there, too. And reconnaissance there was quite interesting as well. Okay. ______ Edgar Grabhorn

(Laughter) Edgar Grabhorn

Oh, yes -- Edgar Grabhorn

What was your feeling about the Vietnam War by the time you left the service? Edgar Grabhorn
I was pretty disappointed. If you got to Saigon, you found that the Bachelor Officer's Quarters and -- were owned by officers from the Vietnam Army; that is, the South Vietnam Army. And these officers didn't do anything but gather in money from their rental for these quarters. They were, well, just to say it bold, I -- I think they were cowardly. I think they were cowardly, and I think they were crafty and not something to be admired. I was very disappointed. And I also felt that we had no chance at all of concluding that war. Well, that seemed to be the feeling that most people who were out there had, too, I think -- Edgar Grabhorn
